title: Theoretical Limitations of Multi-Layer Transformer
authors: Lijie Chen (UC Berkeley, United States), Binghui Peng (Google research, United States), Hongxun Wu (UC Berkeley, United States)
abstract: Transformers, especially the decoder-only variants, are the backbone of most modern large language models. Yet, we have a very limited understanding of their limitations (i.e., what tasks they cannot solve) besides the simplest 1-layer case. Due to the difficulty of analyzing multi-layer models, all previous work relies on unproven complexity conjectures to show limitations for multi-layer Transformers. In this work, we prove the first unconditional lower bound against multi-layer decoder-only transformers. For any constant L, we prove that any L-layer decoder-only transformer needs a polynomial model dimension (n^{O(1)}) to perform sequential composition of L functions over an input of n tokens. As a consequence, our results give: (1) the first depth-width trade-off for multi-layer transformers, exhibiting that the L-step composition task is exponentially harder for L-layer models compared to (L+1)-layer ones; (2) an unconditional separation between encoder and decoder, exhibiting a hard task for decoders that can be solved by an exponentially shallower and smaller encoder; (3) a provable advantage of chain-of-thought, exhibiting a task that becomes exponentially easier when the model is allowed to produce an intermediate sequence of tokens before outputting the final answer. On the technical side, we propose the multi-party autoregressive communication model that abstracts the key aspects of a decoder-only Transformer. In particular, lower bounds within this communication model imply lower bounds against decoder-only transformers, independent of their implementation details. To prove lower bounds in this communication model, we also introduce a new proof technique that finds a certain indistinguishable decomposition of all possible inputs iteratively. We believe our new communication model and proof techniques will be helpful to understand the computational power of transformers further.

Does the architecture have any potential
limitations or weaknesses?
Such limitations shed light on what types of tasks
Transformers could struggle to solve in practice, as well
as potential improvements on the underlying architectures that can be provably better than Transformers (if
they overcome these weaknesses).
Ultimately, we hope to understand what tasks Transformers can or cannot learn to solve within the current
training paradigm. This is challenging to study formally
for two reasons: (1) a significant part of the success
of LLM training is that they are trained on a gigantic
dataset (i.e., the whole Internet), for which we do not
have a good mathematical model. (2) Modern machine
learning optimization algorithms (such as Adam [27] or
AdamW [32]) are often applied to highly non-convex
optimization tasks, making them difficult to analyze
theoretically.
A representational power perspective on Transformers. A cleaner yet still fundamental question is to study
what types of functions Transformers can or cannot
represent: we say a Transformer can represent a function
if one can set the parameters of the Transformer so
that it computes this function. Clearly, if we show
that Transformers cannot represent a particular function,
they also cannot learn such a function, regardless of
the training data and the optimization methods; that is,
by studying its representational power, we bypass the
difficulty in analyzing the optimization algorithms and
the training data.
To study Transformers as a computational model,
we often treat the context length (prompt length) n
as a growing parameter and analyze how the size of
the Transformer must scale to solve a given problem.

Following the convention of [49], we say that a task is

There has been extensive literature on the representation power of the simplest 1-layer Transformers:
We know they cannot solve many basic tasks, such
as the composition of two functions [40], 3SUM [49],
and induction heads [50]. However, for the (arguably)
most relevant case of multi-layer Transformers, unconditional lower bounds remain elusive even for two-layer
models.1 As a result, researchers have turned to study
the computational power of Transformers by assuming
certain conjectures from complexity theory. In particular, researchers have shown limitations of Transformers
relying on assumptions on complexity classes such as
TC0 [37], log-space computation L [40] and Massively
Parallel Computation (MPC) [51]. These assumptions
are however notoriously hard to prove, which brings the
following fundamental question:
Can we establish unconditional limitations
against multi-layer Transformers?
Besides the natural motivation to remove unproven
assumptions, resorting to complexity assumptions often loses the fine-grained structure of the Transformer
model: these works often start by assuming a certain hard
function is hard for a complexity class (such as TC0 )
that can simulate all constant-layer Transformers, which
then implies this hard function cannot be computed by all
constant-layer Transformers. It however fails to provide
a more fine-grained understanding, such as the relative power between Transformers of different constant
depths, as well as the relative power between encoder
and decoder, since these lower bounds would apply to all
of them equally. Jumping ahead, our proof techniques are
fine-grained enough to provide such insights (distinguish
between encoders and decoders, and between different
depths).

B. Implications
Next, we discuss several implications of our main
Theorem I.1.
1) Depth-size tradeoff for Transformer: As mentioned
above, Theorem I.1 highlights the importance of depth
in Transformers. Indeed, it implies an exponential depthsize tradeoff for Transformer architecture. This is because the L-sequential function composition can be easily solved by an (L+1)-layer decoder-only Transformer,
with only polylogarithmic number of parameters (i.e.,
H = O(1), d = poly log(n), p = log(n)).
Corollary I.2 (Depth-size tradeoff). For any constant
L ≥ 1, there exists a task (a.k.a. L-sequential function
composition) such that (1) an (L + 1)-layer Transformer can solve the task with polylogarithmic number
of parameters while (2) any L-layer Transformer needs
polynomial number of parameters to solve the task.
The lower bound on induction heads in [50] gives
a strong separation between the depth-1 and depth-2
transformers. Our results are the first to extend such separations between depth-L and depth-L + 1 transformers
for every constant L ≥ 2.
a) Prior work: depth-size tradeoff for neural networks.: Depth-size (or depth-width) tradeoff has been
extensively studied for neural networks [9], [14], [17],
[28], [30], [33], [35], [47], [48], [54], [56], [57], [66].
Most work has focused on the feed-forward ReLU
network. However, as pointed out by [56], [57], proving

depth-width tradeoff for L ≥ 4 layer ReLU network
faces circuit lower bound and natural proof barriers for
benign functions (i.e., functions that can be computed in
polynomial time and has polynomial-bounded Lipschitz
constant). Hence, existing work [14], [17] either focus on
very shallow network (L = 2, 3), or construct separations
based on high oscillatory function with super-polynomial
Lipscitz constant [54].
2) Separation between Transformer encoder/decoder:
Theorem I.1 also implies a separation between the
encoder and the decoder architecture, since the Lsequential function composition task can be easily solved
by an O(log(L))-layer Transformer encoder.
Corollary I.3 (Separation between encoder and decoder). For any constant L ≥ 1, there exists a task
(a.k.a. L-sequential function composition) such that (1)
an O(log(L))-layer Transformer encoder could solve the
task with polylogarithmic number of parameters while
(2) any L-layer Transformer decoder needs polynomial
number of parameters to solve the task.
There has been a lot of work [2], [3], [20], [38], [44]
comparing the empirical performance of encoder and
decoder architecture, see [53] for a detailed coverage. A
recent work [18] compares the expressive power between
encoder and decoder, showing a strong separation by
assuming a conjecture of the hardness of a certain
triplet counting problem. In contrast, our work gives
the first unconditional separation without any unproven
assumptions.
3) Provable benefits of chain of thought: The chain of
thought (CoT) [61] is known to help with the reasoning
by inducing the LLM to perform step by step reasoning
and eventually leading to the correct answer. Formally,
CoT allows the model to output an intermediate sequence
of tokens (i.e., the reasoning steps) before outputs the
final answer.
Theorem I.1 implies the first provable benefits of CoT,
without relying on any computational complexity conjecture. This is because L-sequential function composition
can be easily solved using L-steps of CoT with only
polylogarithmic number of parameters.
Corollary I.4 (Provably benefits of CoT). For any constant L ≥ 1, there exists a task (a.k.a. L-sequential function composition) such that (1) an one-layer Transformer
with CoT could solve the task with polylogarithmic
number of parameters while (2) any L-layer Transformer
decoder needs polynomial number of parameters to solve
the task.

E. Discussion, limitation and future work
Our paper proves the first unconditional lower bound
on the representational power of multi-layer Transformer, over a sequential composition task that could
naturally arise from practice. Our results offer several
interesting implications regarding the depth-size tradeoff
inherent in Transformer architectures, the representational separation between encoders and decoders and the
substantial impact of employing CoT. These theoretical
insights align well with empirical observations, suggesting that the representational lens contributes meaningfully to understanding Transformer models.

E NCODER LOWER BOUNDS IMPLY CIRCUIT LOWER
BOUNDS

In this section, we will sketch a proof that a lower
bound for encoder-only transformers would imply breakthrough circuit lower bounds against constant-depth
symmetric circuits. A constant-depth symmetric circuit
is a constant depth circuit in which every gate has
unbounded fan-in and computes a symmetric boolean
function on its inputs. A function f is symmetric if
function value f (x) only depends on the number of 1’s
in x.
More formally, we will show that any depth-L symmetric circuit with s wires can be simulated by an
encoder-only transformer of depth 6L and Hdp =
O((s/n)2 ). Therefore, any lower bound of Hdp =

Ω(nϵ ) against encoders is also an Ω(n1+ϵ/2 )-wire lower
bound against symmetric circuits.
Proving lower bounds against constant-depth symmetric circuits is notoriously hard.15 It was shown [46]
that the inner product module 2 function16 requires a
symmetric circuit of Ω(n) gates. However, no non-trivial
lower bounds were known even for O(n)-wire depth-3
symmetric circuits (see, e.g., [55]).17 Therefore, given
our simulation result, if for any ϵ > 0 we can prove
an Ω(nϵ )-size lower bound against depth-18 encoders,
we would get lower bounds against n1+ϵ/2 -wire depth-3
symmetric circuits, which would be a breakthrough in
circuit complexity theory.
On the choice of attention/MLP layers.: Here we
allow the parameters for the attention and MLP layers
to change arbitrarily for different positions (our autoregressive communication model applies to this case as
well). Otherwise, the encoder architecture would only
have poly(Hdp) bits of non-uniformity; an encoder
lower bound of Hdp = Ω(nϵ ) would then follow
directly from the folklore time hierarchy theorem with
advice DTIME(nk+1 ) ̸⊆ DTIME(nk )/o(n) (see, e.g.,
Proposition 1 of [52]).18
Simulating a single symmetric gate.: On input
x1 , x2 , . . . , xn ∈ {0, 1}n , a symmetric gate with w wires
outputs f (xi1 + xi2 + · · · + xiw ) for some fixed function
